Boron and the
Diborane Problem

How one small molecule, B2H6, took thirty years to solve, and why it forced chemists to accept a new kind of chemical bond.

P. A. Mohammed Ziyad · Department of Chemistry, Farook College (Autonomous), Kozhikode

B2H6 · D2h
drag to rotate
Geometry from gas-phase electron diffraction: B–Ht 1.19 Å, B–Hb 1.33 Å, B···B 1.77 Å. K. Wade, Electron Deficient Compounds, Nelson, 1971, Fig. 2-6, p. 13.
Open with the question: how can a molecule with 12 valence electrons hold 8 atoms together? This deck is the history and the evidence. The bonding theory comes in Deck 2. The rotating model is the answer, shown first, so that students can watch the field arrive at it.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this deck you should be able to

  • Explain why a boron atom, with three valence electrons and four valence orbitals, gives electron-deficient compounds.
  • Describe Stock's high-vacuum methods and the first boranes he isolated (1912–1932).
  • State the valence problem posed by B2H6 and outline the main structures proposed for it (1921–1945).
  • Show how magnetism, dipole moment, chemistry, IR, electron diffraction and NMR evidence eliminated every model except the hydrogen-bridged D2h structure.
  • Account for the 12 valence electrons of B2H6 using four 2c–2e and two 3c–2e bonds.
Historical framework: D. M. P. Mingos, "Personal Historical Perspective on the Development of Electron Counting Rules for Boranes and Clusters…", Struct. Bond. 2021, 187, 1–67; P. Laszlo, "A diborane story", Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2000, 39, 2071.
Read the outcomes. Stress outcome 4: students should be able to argue from data to structure, not just recall the answer.
Part A

The element

Three valence electrons, four valence orbitals and very high ionisation energies.

A
Short section on the element itself: why boron is electron-poor.
The element

Boron at a glance

Atomic number, configuration5 · [He]2s²2p¹
Natural isotopes¹⁰B ≈ 20 %, ¹¹B ≈ 80 %
Sum of first three ionisation energies, I1+I2+I36888 kJ mol⁻¹
Covalent radius88 pm
Electronegativity (spectroscopic)2.05
m.p. (β-rhombohedral B)2453 K

Removing all three valence electrons costs 6888 kJ mol⁻¹, so free B³⁺ ions do not form: boron(III) chemistry is covalent.

Crustal abundance (ppm)

Rare overall, but concentrated by geochemistry into rich borate beds (borax, kernite, colemanite). Tourmaline, the most abundant boron mineral, has ≈ 10 % B.

W.-K. Li, G.-D. Zhou, T. C. W. Mak, Adv. Struct. Inorg. Chem., OUP 2008, Table 13.1.1; abundances and minerals: E. L. Muetterties in The Chemistry of Boron and its Compounds, ed. Muetterties, Wiley, 1967, ch. 1, pp. 1–2 (abundance figure as quoted there; modern estimates are ≈ 10 ppm).
Highlight the sum of the first three ionisation energies (6888 kJ/mol). It explains why boron chemistry is covalent, unlike aluminium which forms Al3+ in many salts. Abundance: rare in the crust, but concentrated into workable borate deposits.
The element

From borax to boric acid to boron, 1702–1824

  • 1702, W. Homberg: heating borax with "oil of vitriol" (H2SO4) gave boric acid, sold as sal sedativum Hombergi.
  • 1777: boric acid found in the volcanic hot springs (soffioni) of Tuscany.
  • 1808, H. Davy (London): electrolysis, then reduction of boric acid with potassium. He named the product boracium, expecting a metal.
  • 1808, J. L. Gay-Lussac & L. J. Thénard (Paris): reduction with potassium. They showed by re-oxidation that boric acid is the oxide of the new element, which they named bore.

Both 1808 samples were only ≈ 60 % boron: a grey-olive powder contaminated with metal borides and oxide.

1824 · J. J. Berzelius

Berzelius prepared boron by reducing potassium fluoroborate, KBF4, with potassium, the same fluoride route that gave him silicon from K2SiF6.

His analyses of the fluoride and boric acid gave a consistent combining weight. The product was a non-metal, not Davy's "metal", and this settled boron's status as an element.

Name: borax (Arabic buraq, Persian burah) + the ending of carbon.

N. N. Greenwood, A. Earnshaw, Chemistry of the Elements, 2nd edn, 1997, §6.1; J. J. Berzelius, "Undersökning af flusspatssyran och dess märkvärdigaste föreningar", Kongl. Vetensk. Acad. Handl. 1824; purity (≈ 60 %): Chemicool, "Boron" (chemicool.com); Wikipedia, "Boron" (history).
Stress that boric acid and borax were known long before the element. The 1808 isolations show the period's assumption that "earths" hide metals: Davy expected a metal. Berzelius's contribution was chemical characterisation: reproducible compounds with fixed composition. Ask: why would a 60 % sample still be called an element? Because its oxidation always regenerated the same acid.
The element

A century from discovery to pure boron

YearWhoMethodPurity
1808Davy; Gay-Lussac & ThénardB2O3/H3BO3 + K≈ 60 %
1824BerzeliusKBF4 + Kimpure
1892H. MoissanB2O3 + Mgmuch purer
1909E. Weintraub (GE)BCl3 + H2, electric arc≈ 99 %
todayvan Arkel–de Boer routeBI3 on hot Ta filament> 99.9 %

Why so slow?

Molten boron (m.p. ≈ 2080 °C) attacks almost every container. Traces of O, C, N or metal give hard, refractory borides and suboxides that are almost impossible to separate from the element.

Greenwood & Earnshaw (1997), §6.1–6.2; E. Weintraub, Trans. Am. Electrochem. Soc. 1909, 16, 165; Moissan (1892): Royal Society of Chemistry, Periodic Table: Boron (history).
Purity is the theme. Each method improves the reducing agent or the boron source: K, then Mg, then H2 in an arc. Point out the van Arkel–de Boer transport method, from the same van Arkel who appears later with an ionic structure for diborane. The difficulty of purification foreshadows the borides of Deck 10.
Did you know?

Borax came along the Silk Road

  • In the ancient world borax was known almost only from Tibet, where it crystallised just below the soil around salt lakes.
  • By about 1100 AD goldsmiths used it as a flux: molten borate dissolves metal oxides and keeps metal surfaces clean for soldering.
  • Borates with H2SO4 and methanol give volatile B(OMe)3, which burns with a green flame. Prospectors used this flame test to locate borate deposits.
Greenwood & Earnshaw (1997) §6.1; Muetterties (1967) ch. 1, p. 1. Photographs from course PPT.
Light-hearted aside. The flame test is easy to demonstrate with boric acid, methanol and a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid in a fume hood.
Did you know?

Every plant cell wall is held together by boron

  • Boron is an essential micronutrient for plants. Fruits, vegetables, nuts and pulses are the main dietary sources for humans.
  • In the wall, a borate diester cross-links two chains of the pectin rhamnogalacturonan II (RG-II), holding the network together.
  • Deficiency gives brittle, cracked tissue, for example "hollow heart" in groundnut and heart-rot of beet.
  • Bacteria use a boron-containing signal molecule, AI-2, a furanosyl borate diester, for quorum sensing.
M. Kobayashi, T. Matoh, J. Azuma, Plant Physiol. 1996, 110, 1017; M. A. O'Neill et al., J. Biol. Chem. 1996, 271, 22923; X. Chen et al., Nature 2002, 415, 545 (AI-2).
Use this to link boron's Lewis acidity (next slide) to biology: borate binds cis-diols to give tetrahedral esters. That is the same empty-orbital chemistry, shown in a cell wall. Only a few parts per million in soil separate deficiency from toxicity.

  • Every isolable boron compound is trivalent. BF is known only at high temperature.
  • BX3 is trigonal planar (120°), with one empty 2pz orbital perpendicular to the plane.
  • The empty orbital explains boron's strong acceptor behaviour and the ease of forming tetrahedral BX4⁻ and R3N→BX3.
E. L. Muetterties, in The Chemistry of Boron and its Compounds, Wiley, 1967, ch. 1, §1.3, pp. 3–4; Mingos, Struct. Bond. 2021, 187, 1, Fig. 1. π-Back-donation in BX3 is treated in Deck 2.
Build the orbital boxes step by step. The key idea is one empty p orbital in BX3. Everything that follows (Lewis acidity, dimerisation, multicentre bonding) comes from having more orbitals than electrons.
The element

What "electron deficient" means

Electron-deficient compound: a molecule with too few valence electrons to bind all adjacent atoms by 2-centre, 2-electron (2c–2e) bonds.

  • Typical of atoms with more valence orbitals than valence electrons, such as Li, Be, B, Al and Ga.
  • Typical examples are B2H6 and the higher boranes, Al2Me6, (MeLi)4, (BeH2)n and the carboranes.
  • These atoms adopt structures with more neighbours than electron pairs, using multicentre bonds.
"…the deficiency turned out to be in our understanding of chemical bonding…"K. Wade, Electron Deficient Compounds, 1971, p. 5

Note on usage

Organic chemists use "electron deficient" for a centre at the positive end of a polar bond. Here the term is structural: it counts electrons against links.

K. Wade, Electron Deficient Compounds, Nelson, London, 1971, ch. 1, pp. 1–5; H. C. Longuet-Higgins, Q. Rev. Chem. Soc. 1957, 11, 121.
Define carefully: electron deficiency is a structural statement (fewer electron pairs than links), not a charge statement. Read Wade's line: the deficiency was in our understanding.
Part B

Alfred Stock and the boron hydrides

New compounds needed a new laboratory technique before they could even be studied.

B
Section on the experimentalist who made the field possible.
Stock and the boranes

Alfred Stock (1876–1946)

  • Began work on boron hydrides at Breslau in 1909, and on the silicon hydrides at the same time.
  • Earlier reports of "boron hydride" were of the impure, green-burning gas from acid on metal borides.
  • Between 1912 and 1936 he isolated and characterised B2H6, B4H10, B5H9, B5H11, B6H10 and B10H14.
  • He named them by analogy with the alkanes: borane, silane.
  • His work was summarised in the Baker Lectures at Cornell (1932), published as Hydrides of Boron and Silicon (1933).
"All statements about the hydrides of boron earlier than 1912… are untrue."N. V. Sidgwick (1927), quoted by Mingos (2021)
A. Stock, Hydrides of Boron and Silicon, Cornell Univ. Press, Ithaca, 1933; M. F. Hawthorne, "Boron Hydrides", in Muetterties (ed.), 1967, ch. 5, p. 223; Mingos, Struct. Bond. 2021, 187, 3–4.
Stock's achievement was technical as much as chemical: he isolated six boranes that earlier workers could not even purify. Use Sidgwick's remark to show how complete the break with older work was.
Stock and the boranes

How Stock came to the boron hydrides

1894–99 · Berlin

Doctorate under Emil Fischer on the analytical separation of As and Sb.

1899–1900 · Paris

A year with Henri Moissan, assigned to make "still unknown compounds of boron and silicon". This led to the boron silicides (B3Si, B6Si).

1900s · Berlin

Volatile hydrides of P, As and Sb (e.g. SbH3), his first experience of gaseous, toxic, unstable hydrides.

1909 · Breslau

He turned to the hydrides of boron and silicon together.

Why boron hydrides?

  • Acid on metal borides gave a gas that burned green. Earlier "BH3" reports (Jones & Taylor 1881; Sabatier; Ramsay & Hatfield 1901) were contradictory and of uncertain composition.
  • Carbon, silicon and boron are diagonal and periodic neighbours. Would B and Si form hydride families as rich as the alkanes?
  • No existing method could separate such reactive gases, so he had to build one: the vacuum line.

Outcome

Silanes and boranes became the first binary hydride families to approach the hydrocarbons in variety.

A. Stock, Hydrides of Boron and Silicon, 1933, ch. 1; H. Moissan, A. Stock, C. R. Acad. Sci. 1900, 131, 139 (boron silicides); Wikipedia, "Alfred Stock"; EuChemS, 100 Distinguished European Chemists: Stock.
The point is continuity: Stock's career moved from analytical separation to Moissan's boron and silicon work, and then to volatile hydrides. The boranes were a natural next step for someone with exactly that training. Contradictory older reports were the scientific motive. The lack of a separation technique was the obstacle he solved.
Stock and the boranes

The high-vacuum line: chemistry without air

Problem

Boranes are volatile, toxic and air-sensitive; several ignite spontaneously in air.

Solution

An all-glass line under high vacuum. Mercury valves replace greased stopcocks, which absorb and react with boranes.

Separation

Fractional condensation through traps at falling temperatures separates the hydrides by volatility.

Schematic redrawn; trap temperatures are illustrative. A. Stock, Hydrides of Boron and Silicon, 1933; F. G. A. Stone, Q. Rev. Chem. Soc. 1955, 9, 174 (p. 174); Wade (1971), p. 5.
Explain fractional condensation: the vapour passes through traps at decreasing temperatures and each borane condenses where its vapour pressure becomes negligible. Mercury float valves avoid grease, which absorbs boranes.
Stock and the boranes

From magnesium boride to diborane

1912 · Stock & Massenez

Mg3B2 + HCl(aq) → B4H10 + other boranes + H2

The yield is low (a few per cent of the boron). Tetraborane was the first borane to be fully characterised.

1913 · Stock & Friederici

B4H10 → (warm) B2H6 + higher boranes

Diborane is the simplest isolable borane. Its formula came from analysis and vapour density.

  • Boranes interconvert on heating, as hydrocarbons do on cracking but at lower temperatures. Near 700 °C they decompose completely to B + H2.
  • B2H6 is stable at room temperature (< 10 % decomposition a year) but decomposes quickly at 100 °C.
  • B–H hydrogen is hydridic: B2H6 + 6 H2O → 2 B(OH)3 + 6 H2

Later, better routes

Schlesinger & Burg (1931, BCl3/H2 discharge) and Schlesinger & Brown (1940s, LiBH4/BF3) are covered in Deck 3.

A. Stock, C. Massenez, Ber. Dtsch. Chem. Ges. 1912, 45, 3539; A. Stock, K. Friederici, ibid. 1913, 46, 1959; F. G. A. Stone, Q. Rev. 1955, 9, 174–175; Hawthorne in Muetterties (1967), ch. 5, p. 241.
Two key reactions: hydrolysis of magnesium boride (Stock & Massenez 1912) and thermal conversion of B4H10 to B2H6 (1913). Note that the B–H hydrogen is hydridic: water releases H2.
Stock and the boranes

Stock's boranes fall into two families

BoraneNamem.p. / °Cb.p. / °CFamily
B2H6diborane(6)−165−92.5BnHn+4
B4H10tetraborane(10)−12018BnHn+6
B5H9pentaborane(9)−4760BnHn+4
B5H11pentaborane(11)−12365BnHn+6
B6H10hexaborane(10)−62108BnHn+4
B10H14decaborane(14)99.7213BnHn+4
  • The number in brackets gives the H count: pentaborane(9) vs pentaborane(11).
  • BnHn+4 boranes are the more stable family (later called nido). BnHn+6 boranes are less stable (later arachno).
  • B10H14 is a stable white solid that was the first borane to have its structure solved by X-ray (1950).

Looking ahead

Why these two formulas and no others? The answer is Wade's rules, in Deck 6.

Physical constants: Stone, Q. Rev. 1955, 9, 175 (Table 1) and Greenwood & Earnshaw (1997), §6.3; families: Mingos (2021), p. 4; B10H14: J. S. Kasper, C. M. Lucht, D. Harker, Acta Crystallogr. 1950, 3, 436.
Introduce the BnHn+4 and BnHn+6 families and the bracketed H-count nomenclature. Leave the question open: why only these formulas? Wade's rules answer it in Deck 6.
Stock and the boranes · the next generation

H. I. Schlesinger and the Chicago school

  • Hermann I. Schlesinger (1882–1960), University of Chicago, took up Stock's methods in the late 1920s.
  • 1931, with A. B. Burg: the first practical diborane synthesis.
    2 BCl3 + 5 H2 → B2H5Cl + 5 HCl  (discharge)
    6 B2H5Cl ⇌ 5 B2H6 + 2 BCl3
  • 1935: methylation of B2H6 stops at Me4B2H2, the first chemical hint of two kinds of H.
  • 1940: the metal borohydrides Al(BH4)3, Be(BH4)2 and LiBH4, with B–H–M bridges everywhere.

Why he believed in bridges

In Al(BH4)3 each BH4 is attached to Al through hydrogen. If H can bridge B and Al, it can bridge B and B. He put this to Pauling in 1941 (Part D).

His students

A. B. Burg, borane chemistry at USC; H. C. Brown, hydroboration and the Nobel Prize in 1979 (Deck 5).

H. I. Schlesinger, A. B. Burg, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1931, 53, 4321; H. I. Schlesinger, A. O. Walker, ibid. 1935, 57, 621; H. I. Schlesinger, R. T. Sanderson, A. B. Burg, ibid. 1940, 62, 3421; H. I. Schlesinger, H. C. Brown, ibid. 1940, 62, 3429; Stone, Q. Rev. 1955, 9, 174.
Schlesinger is the bridge between Stock's preparative work and the structural answer. His chemistry, especially the borohydrides, made a bridging hydrogen chemically plausible years before spectroscopy proved it. Keep the 1931 equations for Deck 3, where preparations are compared.
Did you know?

Sodium borohydride was a wartime by-product

  • In 1940–42 the U.S. war effort needed a volatile uranium compound for isotope separation. Schlesinger and Brown made U(BH4)4, the most volatile U compound after UF6.
  • Scale-up needed a convenient source of BH4⁻. This gave a new reagent:
    4 NaH + B(OMe)3 → NaBH4 + 3 NaOMe
  • UF6 won for uranium. NaBH4, published in 1953 after declassification, became one of the most widely used reducing agents in chemistry.
BH4⁻

tetrahedral, isoelectronic with CH4
B–H 1.21 Å

Reduces aldehydes and ketones in water or alcohol: a hydride donor that is stable in protic solvent.

H. I. Schlesinger, H. C. Brown et al., J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1953, 75, 186–224 (series); H. C. Brown, Nobel Lecture 1979, Science 1980, 210, 485; B–H in BH4⁻: Greenwood & Earnshaw (1997), §6.3.
Students know NaBH4 from organic chemistry; few know it came out of boron hydride research and the Manhattan Project. Brown's later hydroboration chemistry, his Nobel work, grew directly from this programme.
Did you know?

The vacuum line poisoned its inventor

  • Stock's mercury pumps, valves and manometers gave his laboratory a constant mercury-vapour atmosphere.
  • For years he suffered headaches, memory loss and fatigue before he recognised chronic mercury poisoning in himself and his co-workers.
  • His 1926 paper "Die Gefährlichkeit des Quecksilberdampfes" (the dangers of mercury vapour) was one of the first warnings of the hazards of low-level mercury exposure, including from dental amalgams.
Hg

Vapour pressure at 20 °C ≈ 0.16 Pa,
enough to saturate laboratory air well above safe limits.

Lesson: a new technique brings new hazards.

A. Stock, Z. Angew. Chem. 1926, 39, 461; vapour pressure of Hg: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics.
Stock's mercury poisoning is a real case study in laboratory safety. He turned his own illness into a research programme on micromercurialism.
Part C

The diborane puzzle, 1912–1945

Stock knew the formula, but no one could draw the molecule.

C
From here the deck follows how chemists thought, proposal by proposal.
The puzzle

Count the electrons

2 B × 3+6 H × 1=12 e
7 bonds × 2=14 e
  • B2H6 has only 6 electron pairs for 7 links in any ethane-like structure, and 8 links in a bridged one.
  • C2H6 has 14 electrons. B2H6 is isoelectronic with C2H4, not ethane.
  • BH3 itself was unknown, and it is BH3 that dimerises (ΔHdiss ≈ 150 kJ mol⁻¹).
L. Pauling, The Nature of the Chemical Bond, Cornell Univ. Press, 1939, ch. 8 ("The one-electron bond. The hydrides of boron"), quoted in Mingos (2021), p. 5; dissociation enthalpy: Wade (1971), p. 14.
Do the count with the class: 2×3 + 6×1 = 12 electrons, but an ethane-like molecule needs 14. Note the isoelectronic relation to C2H4. Students should leave knowing exactly what the "problem" was.
The puzzle

Two candidate geometries

"Ethane-like" · D3d
drag to rotate
  • Six equivalent H. Has a B–B bond. C3 axis along B–B.
  • Supported by Stock, Bauer (1937) and most theorists before 1943.
Hydrogen-bridged · D2h
drag to rotate
  • Four terminal Ht and two bridging Hb. C2 axis along B···B.
  • Proposed by Dilthey (1921). Confirmed 1943–1951.
Symmetry elements: Wade (1971), Figs 2-1 and 2-2, pp. 7–8. Models drawn from experimental (D2h) and idealised tetrahedral (D3d) coordinates.
Rotate both models. Ask students to find the C3 axis in the ethane-like model and the C2 axis in the bridged one. These symmetry differences become decisive in the IR section.

Wade (1971), §2-2; Mingos (2021), pp. 3–7; P. Laszlo, Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2000, 39, 2071; W. N. Lipscomb, Nobel Lecture, Science 1977, 196, 1047.
Overview before the detail. Teal events move towards the bridge, grey ones away from it. Note the long detour of 1928–1937 when the best theorists backed the wrong framework.
The puzzle · how they thought

What any structure for B2H6 had to satisfy

The facts (to 1930)

  • Formula B2H6, with 12 valence electrons
  • Volatile (b.p. −92.5 °C), so molecular, not a salt
  • Forms B2H6·2NH3, behaving as a "dibasic" partner
  • Higher boranes B4H10, B5H9 … also need a pattern

The theoretical toolkit

Ionic bondKossel 1916
Electron-pair bond, octetLewis 1916; Langmuir 1919
Hydride displacementGrimm 1925
One-electron bondSidgwick, Sugden 1927
Resonance, MO theoryPauling, Mulliken 1928–39

Read every proposal as

① which rule it tried to save, ② where it put the 12 electrons, ③ which later fact killed it.

Mingos, Struct. Bond. 2021, 187, pp. 4–6; G. N. Lewis, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1916, 38, 762; I. Langmuir, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1919, 41, 868; Laszlo (2000).
This slide sets the method for the next dozen slides. Each proposal is an attempt to keep a cherished rule (the octet, the electron pair, carbon analogy) while fitting a formula that seems to break it. Ask students to fill the three columns as each proposal appears.
The puzzle · proposals · 1921

Dilthey (1921): the bridge, twenty years too early

11 Nov 1921 · W. Dilthey, Chemical Society of Erlangen

B2H6 as two BH2 units joined by two shared H, each B tetravalent and tetrahedral.

His reasoning

  • Stock's chemistry suggested boron was four-coordinate in its hydrides.
  • Tetrahedral B, by analogy with C, fixes the geometry, and two H must then be shared.

Why it was ignored

  • It was a structural proposal only, with no account of where the 12 electrons go.
  • A hydrogen bonded to two atoms contradicted the Lewis–Langmuir picture of H as univalent.
W. Dilthey, Z. Angew. Chem. 1921, 34, 596; Wade (1971), p. 6; Mingos (2021), p. 4.
Dilthey got the geometry right in 1921, but geometry without electrons was not persuasive in the age of Lewis structures. This is a good place to discuss why a correct idea can fail: it lacked a mechanism, and it violated a rule (univalent H) that had served chemistry well.
The puzzle · proposals · 1922

Huggins (1922): boranes as unsaturated hydrocarbons

  • Huggins objected to Stock's tetravalent boron. Why should B be four-valent only in its hydrides?
  • He kept B trivalent and paired each borane with a hydrocarbon:
    B2H6 ~ ethylene, B4H10 ~ butadiene, B6H12 ~ benzene, B10H14 ~ naphthalene.
  • He proposed a 4-electron bond shared by four atoms: the "residual affinity" of a double bond holds extra H, more strongly for B than for C.

What to notice

This is the first multicentre bond idea for boranes, with electrons shared over more than two atoms. B6H12 was a spurious compound, a warning against building theory on unverified formulas.

M. L. Huggins, "Boron hydrides", J. Phys. Chem. 1922, 26; reviewed in Bauer, Chem. Rev. 1942, 31, 43 and Laszlo (2000).
Huggins is often forgotten, but his "four-electron bond shared by four atoms" anticipates multicentre bonding by two decades. His aromatic analogies are wrong in detail, but notice the instinct: delocalisation, as in benzene, is how chemistry handles "too few" localised bonds.
The puzzle · proposals · 1922–1925

Chasing the octet: Böeseken, Henstock, Wahl

1923 · H. Henstock

Henstock's electron arrangement of the B2 core (H omitted), via course PPT

  • One B keeps a sextet and carries 2 H. The other completes an octet and carries 4 H.
  • The octet boron is then bonded to five atoms (4 H + B), which was unprecedented in 1923.
1922 · J. Böeseken; 1925 · W. A. Wahl
  • Avoids five-coordinate B by moving one H out as H⁺: a [B2H5]⁻ anion in which both borons have octets.
  • Rejected by Stock: B2H6·2NH3 showed diborane was dibasic, but this formula is monobasic.

Pattern

Each proposal saves the octet by paying elsewhere: five-coordinate boron, or ionisation that the physical properties do not support.

Proposals as reviewed by Bauer, Chem. Rev. 1942, 31, 43 and Laszlo (2000); electron-dot formulae redrawn from figures in the course PPT.
These two proposals show how strongly chemists held the octet. Henstock accepts a strange coordination number to keep it; Böeseken and Wahl accept an ion. Stock's test with ammonia, counting how many NH3 add, is a nice example of chemical reasoning about acidity being used to discriminate structures.
The puzzle · proposals · 1924–1927

Diborane as a salt: van Arkel & de Boer, Ulmann

1924 · A. E. van Arkel & J. H. de Boer

(B³⁺)2(H⁻)6: six H⁻ capture all six boron valence electrons, so every particle has a He shell.

1927 · Ulmann

B³⁺ and B⁵⁻ (Ne shell), with 2 H⁻ and 4 H⁺. This is equivalent to a polar [BH2]⁺[BH4]⁻.

Their reasoning

  • Electrostatics (Kossel) worked for salts. Make every particle a closed shell and the electron count is automatically satisfied.

Why it failed

  • B2H6 boils at −92.5 °C. A salt would be an involatile solid.
  • The sum of the first three ionisation energies, I1 + I2 + I3 = 6888 kJ mol⁻¹, makes B³⁺ impossible.
  • Stock & Müller (1927) found no ionic behaviour, and μ = 0 (1935) excludes the polar form.

A grain of truth

[H2B(NH3)2]⁺[BH4]⁻ forms when NH3 cleaves B2H6 (Deck 5).

Figures from course PPT; proposals as reviewed by Bauer, Chem. Rev. 1942, 31, 43 and Laszlo (2000); A. Stock, W. Müller, Ber. 1927, 60, 610 (as cited in course PPT); volatility: Wade (1971), p. 6; ionisation energies: Li, Zhou, Mak (2008), Table 13.1.1.
Ionic models are the simplest way to "satisfy" closed shells, which is why they appeared. Students should be able to kill them with one number, the boiling point, and one thermochemical argument. The NH3 adduct remark shows that ionic forms exist when a base supplies electrons.
The puzzle · proposals · 1927

Core (1927): two kinds of hydrogen, electrons included

outer B–H: 2 e
inner B···H: 1 e
each B: 6 e
  • Outer H (4) share an electron pair with one boron, as normal bonds.
  • Inner H (2) share one electron with each boron. Both electrons of an inner H are attracted by both boron nuclei.
  • Count: 4 × 2 + 4 × 1 = 12 e in 8 links. Each B has a sextet, not an octet.
  • Core argued B2H6 is lower in energy than 2 BH3, assuming BH3 existed.
A. F. Core, "Chemical combination and the constitution of boron hydride", J. Soc. Chem. Ind. 1927, 46, 642–643; Mingos (2021), p. 4. Electron-dot diagram redrawn after course PPT.
Core is the electronic complement of Dilthey: right idea about two kinds of H, and a real electron distribution, but no geometry. In octet terms the borons are only sextets, which is exactly why 1927 chemists found it unattractive. Compare with the modern 3c–2e picture at the end of the deck: Core's two one-electron links per bridge are, in effect, one two-electron three-centre bond.
The puzzle · proposals · 1927

Sugden and Sidgwick (1927): the one-electron bond

  • Sugden found parachor values for PCl5 and SbCl5 that suggested "singlet links", and extended the idea to boranes.
  • Sidgwick kept an ethane-like H3B–BH3 with seven links: five normal bonds and two one-electron B–H bonds.
  • The B 1s ("K") electrons could not be used: that would cost "an impossibly great expenditure of energy".
S. Sugden, J. Chem. Soc. 1927, 1173; N. V. Sidgwick, The Electronic Theory of Valency, Clarendon Press, 1927, p. 103; figures via course PPT.
Sidgwick's reasoning is a model of electron bookkeeping: count the electrons, recognise that the 1s pair is unavailable, and conclude that two links must be one-electron. The proposal is testable: unpaired, one-electron bonds imply magnetism. Hold that thought for 1934.
The puzzle · proposals · 1928

Glockler (1928): BH as a "pseudo-carbon"

Grimm's hydride displacement law (1925), extended to boron

CNOFNeNa+-like
atomCNOFNeNa
+1 HBHCHNHOHFH
+2 HBH2CH2NH2OH2FH2⁺
+3 HBH3CH3NH3OH3⁺
+4 HBH4CH4NH4⁺

Read down a column: each pseudo-atom has the same number of valence electrons as the element at the top. Grimm's law excluded boron, and the boron entries are Glockler's extension.

Glockler's predicted "hydroborons"

HydrocarbonHydroboronSeries
ethane CH3–CH3BH4–BH4 (unknown)BnH3n+2
ethylene CH2=CH2BH3=BH3 "borethane" = B2H6BnH3n
acetylene CH≡CHBH2≡BH2 (unknown)BnH3n−2
  • Electron counts work perfectly: B2H6 is isoelectronic with C2H4.
  • Prediction failed: no B2H8 or B2H4, and Stock's series are BnHn+4 and BnHn+6, not BnH3n.
G. Glockler, "The structure of boron hydrides", Science 1928, 68, 305; H. G. Grimm, Z. Elektrochem. 1925, 31, 474; discussed in G. A. Patani, E. J. LaVoie, Chem. Rev. 1996, 96, 3147. (Course PPT spells "Glocker".)
Grimm's law is the ancestor of isosterism and bioisosterism in drug design, which is why Patani and LaVoie cite it. Glockler's extension correctly sees B2H6 as isoelectronic with ethylene; the same insight resurfaces in Pitzer's protonated double bond (1945). The failed series predictions show the limit of pure electron counting without geometry.
The puzzle · proposals · 1928–1945

Wiberg (1928) to Pitzer (1945): protons in a double bond

  • 1928, E. Wiberg: each B captures electrons to reach a Ne-like octet. Four H are normal B–H bonds; a B=B double bond holds the other two H nuclei electrostatically.
  • Wiberg later (1936) wrote B2H6 as a weak dibasic acid H2[B2H4], to explain B2H6·2NH3.
  • It accounts for diamagnetism (all shells closed) and μ = 0.
  • 1945, K. S. Pitzer: the "protonated double bond". [B2H4]²⁻ is isoelectronic with C2H4, with two protons embedded in the π cloud above and below the B=B axis.

Key insight

Pitzer's nuclei are in the same D2h positions as Dilthey's bridge. Longuet-Higgins later recast the picture as 3-centre MOs.

Wiberg as reviewed by Bauer, Chem. Rev. 1942, 31, 43 and Laszlo (2000); K. S. Pitzer, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1945, 67, 1126; Mingos (2021), pp. 8–11, Figs 3–4; figures via course PPT.
Wiberg's model survives longest among the pre-war ideas because it explains the magnetic and dipole data. Its weakness is the B–B distance: a double bond should be short, and Bauer (1937) found no shortening. Pitzer revives it in 1945 in a form that is geometrically identical to the bridge. Show students that the "protonated double bond" and the "3c–2e bridge" are two languages for one structure.
The puzzle · proposals · 1929

Hellriegel (1929): borrowing the inner electrons

  • Each H3B: unit has its three B–H pairs. The link between the borons (~) was to come from the boron K-shell (1s) electrons.
  • This solved the shortage of electrons by drawing on electrons that valence theory treats as unavailable.
  • Fatal flaw: involving 1s electrons costs hundreds of eV. Sidgwick had already ruled it out as an "impossibly great expenditure of energy".

Lesson

Electron counting uses valence electrons only. Any model that needs core electrons is wrong for a light element.

W. Hellriegel (1929) as reviewed in Bauer, Chem. Rev. 1942, 31, 43 and Laszlo (2000); Sidgwick (1927), p. 103; figure via course PPT.
A short slide. Hellriegel shows how far chemists would go to avoid electron-deficient bonding. Use it to reinforce valence versus core electrons: boron's 1s ionisation energy is about 190 eV, far beyond chemical energies.
The puzzle · proposals · 1932–1939

The ethane-like consensus: Mulliken, Lewis, Pauling

  • Mulliken (1932–33): an MO version of the ethane-like molecule, which predicted paramagnetism.
  • Lewis (1933): all electrons paired, but each pair occupies a link only 6/7 of the time, with 6 pairs spread over 7 links.
  • Pauling (1939): two one-electron bonds resonating among all seven positions. This was the standard textbook answer for a decade.
  • All three accept the ethane-like nuclear framework, supported by the 1925 X-ray and 1937 ED data, and only argue about the electrons.

By 1931 only two survived

The ethane-like one-electron-bond model and Wiberg's double bond. Physical measurements would now decide.

G. N. Lewis, J. Chem. Phys. 1933, 1, 17; L. Pauling, The Nature of the Chemical Bond, Cornell, 1939, ch. 8; S. H. Bauer, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1937, 59, 1096; Mingos (2021), Fig. 2; figures via course PPT.
This is the most authoritative wrong answer in the story: three of the greatest theorists of the century accepted an ethane-like skeleton because the diffraction data seemed to require it. Their disagreement was only about the electrons. Emphasise that theory was constrained by bad structural data.
Part D

Evidence decides

Six independent kinds of measurement, each ruling out at least one model.

D
Now the physical and chemical measurements that settled the question.

The last two columns are the same geometry. Experiment fixes the nuclei, and the bonding description (protonated double bond vs. 3c–2e bridges) is the subject of Deck 2.

Compiled from Wade (1971), §2-2; Mingos (2021), pp. 6–7; Bauer, Chem. Rev. 1942, 31, 43; primary references are given on the following slides.
Reveal row by row. Ask students to predict each verdict before revealing it. The final point is that the last two columns are the same geometry with different bonding descriptions.
Evidence

Two simple measurements, two models eliminated

1934 · L. Farkas & H. Sachsse

B2H6 is diamagnetic

  • Measured indirectly through the catalysis of para-H2 → ortho-H2 conversion. Paramagnetic molecules catalyse it and B2H6 does not.
  • This ruled out Mulliken's paramagnetic one-electron-bond model.
  • Wiberg used the result to support his closed-shell double-bond model.
1935 · K. L. Ramaswamy, IISc Bangalore

B2H6 has no dipole moment

  • Dielectric constant of the vapour, measured on ≈ 100 mL of Stock's own diborane.
  • μ = 0 implies a centrosymmetric molecule, ruling out [BH2]⁺[BH4]⁻ and other unsymmetrical structures.
  • Both D3d and D2h have an inversion centre, so this test cannot decide between them.
L. Farkas, H. Sachsse, Trans. Faraday Soc. 1934, 30, 331; K. L. Ramaswamy, Proc. Indian Acad. Sci. 1935, 2A, 630; interpretation: Laszlo (2000); Bauer (1942). (Course PPT: correct "Sachsee" → Sachsse.)
Two quick, decisive measurements. Diamagnetism removes models with unpaired electrons; zero dipole removes unsymmetrical models. Neither distinguishes D3d from D2h.
Evidence · 1935

Ramaswamy (1935): measuring the dipole moment of B2H6

Debye plot, schematic

  • Method: dielectric constant ε of the vapour at several temperatures gives the molar polarisation PM.
  • Debye equation: PM = (NA/3ε0)(α + μ²/3kT), so a plot of PM against 1/T has slope ∝ μ².
  • Sample: about 100 mL of diborane from Stock's laboratory. He measured volatile B and F compounds in the same study.
  • Result: μ ≈ 0. B2H6 must be centrosymmetric.

What it decides, and what it cannot

It kills [BH2]⁺[BH4]⁻ and Henstock-type forms. It cannot separate the ethane-like D3d and bridged D2h structures, because both have a centre of inversion.

K. L. Ramaswamy, "Dielectric coefficients of volatile compounds of fluorine and boron", Proc. Indian Acad. Sci. 1935, 2A, 630; Debye relation: P. Atkins, J. de Paula, Physical Chemistry, ch. on molecular interactions.
A good place to revise the Debye equation from physical chemistry. Draw the two lines and ask which models survive a zero slope. Then ask why the test cannot distinguish D3d from D2h: both contain an inversion centre. This sets up why spectroscopy (IR selection rules) was needed.
Did you know?

Two contributions from outside Europe and America

Bangalore, 1935

K. L. Ramaswamy at the Indian Institute of Science measured the dielectric constant of diborane and other volatile B and F compounds.

His zero dipole moment was one of the first physical measurements to constrain the shape of B2H6.

Moscow, 1941

Y. K. Syrkin and M. E. Dyatkina gave a correct electron-diffraction analysis of the bridged D2h structure ten years before Hedberg & Schomaker.

Wartime isolation, and later the Soviet "anti-resonance" campaign of 1949–51, kept it out of the Western literature.

K. L. Ramaswamy, Proc. Indian Acad. Sci. 1935, 2A, 630; Y. K. Syrkin, M. E. Dyatkina, Acta Physicochim. URSS 1941, 14, 547; Mingos (2021), p. 7; A. A. Pechenkin, LLULL 1995, 18, 135.
Two contributions often omitted from Western textbooks. Syrkin and Dyatkina had the correct ED structure in 1941; politics, not science, delayed its acceptance.
Evidence · data that misled

Diffraction data that pointed the wrong way

1925 · Mark & Pohland, X-ray

X-rays scatter from electrons, and H has only one. The sample was also polycrystalline.

1937 · S. H. Bauer, gas electron diffraction
  • Bauer used λ = 0.0613 Å electrons and concluded the structure was "ethane-like".
  • Why it misled: H scatters weakly, and the trial models were built on hydrocarbons.
H. Mark, E. Pohland, Z. Kristallogr. 1925, 62, 103; S. H. Bauer, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1937, 59, 1096; Wade (1971), pp. 6–7; Mingos (2021), p. 5. Figures reproduced from the original papers via course PPT.
Two diffraction experiments, both technically competent, both misleading for the same reason: hydrogen scatters weakly. In 1925 the B–B distance was already about right (1.8 Å).
Evidence · 1937

Bauer (1937): a good experiment, the wrong structure

Bauer, JACS 1937, 59, 1096 (extracts; highlight from course PPT).

  • Data: ED curves of B2H6 closely resemble those of C2H6. Fitted with an ethane-like model, B–B ≈ 1.86 Å and B–H ≈ 1.27 Å.
  • Inference 1: B–H is longer than in diatomic BH (1.226 Å), so every bond is weaker than single.
  • Inference 2: no B–B shortening, so no double bond. This eliminates Wiberg's structure.
  • Interpretation: resonance among the seven Sidgwick/Lewis arrangements, each bond about 6/7 single.

What went wrong

H scatters electrons weakly, and the ED analysis needs a trial model. Bauer only tested hydrocarbon-like ones. Hedberg & Schomaker (1951) refitted with the bridge and it fitted better.

S. H. Bauer, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1937, 59, 1096; S. H. Bauer, Chem. Rev. 1942, 31, 43; K. Hedberg, V. Schomaker, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1951, 73, 1482; Mingos (2021), p. 5.
Bauer's reasoning is internally consistent: given an ethane skeleton, long B–H bonds suggest fractional bonds, and resonance spreads them out. The error is upstream, in the trial geometry. This is a powerful lesson on model-dependence in diffraction analysis.
Evidence

Chemistry counts the hydrogens: only four can be replaced

B2H6 + BMe3 → MenB2H6−n  (n = 1–4)

  • Even with a large excess of BMe3, n never exceeds 4.
  • The limiting product is Me2BH2BMe2:
    H2BH2BH2 + 4 R3B → 3 R2BH2BR2
  • So two of the six hydrogens are chemically different. They are the bridging ones.
  • In an ethane-like molecule all six H would be equivalent and Me6B2 should form.
H. I. Schlesinger, A. O. Walker, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1935, 57, 621; Wade (1971), p. 10; Hawthorne in Muetterties (1967), ch. 5, pp. 245–246.
Step through the substitution: four terminal H are replaced, the bridging pair never is. A chemical argument for two kinds of H, years before spectroscopy proved it.
Evidence · a correspondence, 1941

A chemist's hunch meets a theorist's doubt

H. I. Schlesinger → L. Pauling

Schlesinger's sketch: the two borons joined through "an unusual type of hydrogen bond".

"…a structure for diborane quite different from those generally proposed would aid in correlating many of the observations…"

His evidence came from the metal borohydrides and alkyl substitution.

Pauling's reply
"I do not feel very friendly toward the structure which you mention…"
  • The B–B stretching force constant seemed too large for a molecule without a direct B–B bond.
  • The proposal was "vague and indefinite", with no electron distribution.

Who was right?

Schlesinger on the geometry. Pauling had a point too: the bridge bonds contain substantial B–B bonding, with B···B only about 0.15 Å longer than a B=B double bond.

Schlesinger–Pauling correspondence, 1941 (Ava Helen and Linus Pauling Papers, Oregon State University), quoted as in the course PPT; B–B argument: Mingos (2021), p. 8.
Read both quotes aloud. This exchange is valuable because it shows the reasoning of two first-rate chemists from different traditions. The preparative chemist trusts patterns of reactivity; the theorist trusts a quantitative vibrational argument. The final MO picture vindicates both.
Evidence · spectroscopy

Why spectroscopy can decide: symmetry

PredictionD3d (ethane-like)D2h (bridged)
distinct vibrational fundamentals1218
IR-active fundamentals (dipole change)58
B–H stretching bands expected24
axis through the heavy atomsC3C2
Wade (1971), Figs 2-1 and 2-2, pp. 7–9 (figures reproduced). Wade's text writes "D2d" for the ethane-like model on p. 7; staggered ethane is D3d (his Fig. 2-2).
Revise point groups briefly. The key teaching idea is that a structure determines a set of predictions (band counts, selection rules, rotational statistics) that can be checked independently. Both have a centre of symmetry, so the rule of mutual exclusion applies to both, but the counts differ.
Evidence · infrared

The infrared spectrum of B2H6 (900–3000 cm⁻¹)

Band≈ cm⁻¹Assignment
ν82620BH2 (terminal) asym. stretch
ν162525BH2 (terminal) sym. stretch
ν131850bridge B–Hb–B stretch
ν171600bridge B–Hb–B stretch
ν181175BH2 in-plane bend
ν14975BH2 wag
  • Four B–H stretches, twice the number possible for D3d.
  • ν(B–Ht) is near 2600 cm⁻¹, as in normal B–H single bonds. ν(B–Hb) lies between 1500 and 2000 cm⁻¹, showing weaker bridge bonds.
Wade (1971), pp. 7–9, Fig. 2-3 (figure reproduced); frequencies ν8, ν16, ν18, ν14 from W. C. Price, J. Chem. Phys. 1948, 16, 894, Table I; ν13, ν17 read from Wade's figure; H. C. Longuet-Higgins, R. P. Bell, J. Chem. Soc. 1943, 250.
Walk across the spectrum from right to left. Students should identify two terminal stretches near 2600 and two strong bridge stretches near 1600 to 1850 cm−1. The bridge region is almost empty for normal compounds, which makes it diagnostic for B–H–B in any borane. That is a practical tool for Decks 3 and 4.
Evidence · infrared

The vibrations behind the bands, and what they prove

  • Too many bands for ethane-like: the extras are too intense, and at the wrong frequencies, to be overtones or combinations.
  • All bands fit D2h: 8 IR-active of 18 fundamentals.
  • B2D6 shows the expected isotopic shifts (νH/νD ≈ √2 for H-dominated modes), confirming the assignments.
  • Force constants: B–Ht is a normal single bond. B–Hb is considerably weaker.

Chemical corollary

The IR spectra also explain the methylation result. Terminal and bridging H are different, and only terminal H are replaced.

Wade (1971), pp. 8–10, Fig. 2-3; F. Stitt, J. Chem. Phys. 1940, 8, 981; 1941, 9, 780; Longuet-Higgins & Bell (1943); W. C. Price, J. Chem. Phys. 1947, 15, 614.
Point to the bridge stretches: the bridging H moves along the B···B direction (ν17) or perpendicular to it (ν13). Students can derive the √2 isotope ratio from the reduced mass. Emphasise the logic: band count gives the point group, isotopic shifts confirm the assignments, and force constants give bond strength.
Evidence · 1947–1948

Price (1947–48): diborane's spectrum looks like ethylene's

Type (C2H4 label)C2H4B2H6
ν9 CH stretch (b2u)3105.52620
ν11 CH stretch (b3u)2989.52527
ν12 CH2 bend (b3u)1443.51175
ν7 wag (b1u)949.2974

Price, J. Chem. Phys. 1948, 16, 894, Table I (cm⁻¹). The terminal BH2 groups move like the CH2 groups of ethylene.

  • Price resolved the rotational fine structure of the perpendicular bands near 2600 and 970 cm⁻¹. The lines show a clear alternation of intensity.
  • Intensity alternation is a nuclear-spin statistics effect from a C2 axis exchanging identical nuclei. With C3, every third line would be affected.

Later high-resolution work (0.04 cm⁻¹, ¹⁰B/¹¹B-enriched samples) gave moments of inertia, and from them the bond lengths.

W. C. Price, J. Chem. Phys. 1947, 15, 614; 1948, 16, 894; K. S. Pitzer (1945) on the ethylene analogy; W. J. Lafferty, A. G. Maki, T. D. Coyle, J. Mol. Spectrosc. 1970, 33, 345; Wade (1971), p. 10. Line pattern schematic.
Two independent arguments in one paper: (1) band-by-band correspondence with ethylene, matching the D2h symmetry and Glockler's isoelectronic idea; (2) nuclear-spin statistics in the rotational lines, which reveal the order of the principal rotation axis. Mention that rotational analysis later delivered precise bond lengths.
Did you know?
HCLH

The bridged structure was argued by an undergraduate

  • H. Christopher Longuet-Higgins (1923–2004) was a Balliol College, Oxford undergraduate when he and his tutor R. P. Bell published "The structure of the boron hydrides" (1943).
  • They showed that the vibrational spectra fit D2h, and suggested the same bridge in Al and Ga compounds.
  • He went on to theoretical chemistry at Cambridge, and later founded the field of cognitive science at Edinburgh.
H. C. Longuet-Higgins, R. P. Bell, J. Chem. Soc. 1943, 250; Mingos (2021), p. 6; biographical: M. Steedman, "Christopher Longuet-Higgins", Univ. Edinburgh memoir. Portrait: place portraits/longuet-higgins.jpg beside this file.
Longuet-Higgins was about 19 or 20. The story encourages students: careful reasoning about symmetry and spectra, not seniority, solved the problem.
Evidence

NMR, 1955: counting neighbours directly

  • ¹¹B has I = 3/2. An H on one ¹¹B gives a 1:1:1:1 quartet.
  • An H on two ¹¹B nuclei gives a septet of intensities 1:2:3:4:3:2:1.
  • ¹¹B-decoupled spectrum: two singlets in a 2 : 1 ratio (4 Ht : 2 Hb). Hb appears at higher field.
  • ¹¹B spectrum: a triplet of triplets. An ethane-like BH3 would give a 1:3:3:1 quartet.
  • J(¹¹B–Ht) ≈ 135 Hz ≫ J(¹¹B–Hb) ≈ 46 Hz, again showing the weaker bridge bonds.
J. N. Shoolery, Discuss. Faraday Soc. 1955, 19, 215; Wade (1971), pp. 10–13, Figs 2-4 and 2-5. Stick spectra schematic, not to scale.
Build the stick spectra step by step. The 2nI+1 rule with I = 3/2 gives 4 lines for one boron and 7 for two. The decoupled 2:1 ratio counts terminal and bridging H directly.
Evidence · NMR as recorded

The real spectra: decoupling and higher field

  • 30 MHz, coupled: the Ht quartet and Hb septet overlap.
  • ¹¹B decoupled (irradiated at 9.6257 MHz): two peaks, 2 : 1. Hb is at higher field than Ht.
  • 100 MHz: multiplets compress, because shifts scale with field and J does not. Each Hb line splits into a quintet from weak coupling to the 4 Ht.
Wade (1971), pp. 10–13, Figs 2-4, 2-5 (figures reproduced); J. N. Shoolery, Discuss. Faraday Soc. 1955, 19, 215.
Connect the idealised stick spectra from the previous slide with these real traces. Explain double resonance (decoupling) physically: the protons see an average 11B spin state. The quintet on Hb at 100 MHz is the most direct proof that each bridge H is near all four terminal H.
Evidence

The structure, measured three ways

MethodB–HtB–HbB···BHtBHtHbBHb
Electron diffraction119133177119°97°
IR (rotational)120132176121°96°
X-ray (crystal)108125176122°90°

Distances in pm. B–Hb–B ≈ 83°.

Why does X-ray give shorter B–H?

X-rays locate the centre of electron density, not the nucleus. The single electron of a bonded H is pulled towards boron, so the apparent B–H is too short by ≈ 5 pm (Jones & Lipscomb).

Wade (1971), Fig. 2-6, pp. 13–14; ED: K. Hedberg, V. Schomaker, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1951, 73, 1482 and later work; IR: W. J. Lafferty, A. G. Maki, T. D. Coyle, J. Mol. Spectrosc. 1970, 33, 345; X-ray: D. S. Jones, W. N. Lipscomb, Acta Crystallogr. A 1970, 26, 196.
Compare the three methods. ED and IR agree within 1–2 pm; X-ray B–H is about 10 pm short because X-rays locate electron density, which is displaced towards boron for a bonded H.

Verdict

Independent methods agree. B2H6 is the hydrogen-bridged D2h molecule proposed by Dilthey in 1921 and the geometry of Pitzer's protonated double bond. Electron counting is still to come (Part E).

Wade (1971), §2-2 and Fig. 2-6. Note: Wade (p. 13) gives 1:2:2:1 for the ¹¹B quartet expected for BH3; the binomial ratio for three equivalent protons is 1:3:3:1.
This is the slide to return to in revision. Ask students to cover the right-hand column and derive each conclusion from the observation. Point out the minor error in Wade's text about the expected quartet intensities; the correct ratio for coupling to three equivalent spin-1/2 nuclei is 1:3:3:1.
Part E

A new kind of bond

Two electrons shared by three atoms.

E
Having fixed the structure, account for the electrons.
A new kind of bond

Twelve electrons, six bonds, eight links

step 1

Four terminal B–Ht bonds, normal 2c–2e: 4 × 2 = 8 e

step 2

Two B–Hb–B bridges, each a 3-centre, 2-electron bond: 2 × 2 = 4 e

8+4=12 e ✓

What changed

Two electrons now bind three atoms. Each B uses its four sp³-like orbitals: two for Ht and two for the bridges. The MO basis, and the "banana bond", come in Deck 2.

H. C. Longuet-Higgins, R. P. Bell, J. Chem. Soc. 1943, 250; H. C. Longuet-Higgins, Q. Rev. 1957, 11, 121; W. H. Eberhardt, B. Crawford, W. N. Lipscomb, J. Chem. Phys. 1954, 22, 989; Wade (1971), §2-3.
Step 1: four ordinary B–Ht bonds use 8 electrons. Step 2: the remaining 4 electrons form two three-centre two-electron bridges. Compare with Core (1927): his two one-electron links per bridge become one two-electron three-centre bond.
A new kind of bond · aside

Bridges with two electrons, and with four

Al2Me6

CH3 bridges, 3c–2e. Each bridging C has only one orbital pointing at the two Al.

Al···Al ≈ 2.60 Å, close enough for some Al–Al bonding. Al–Cb–Al ≈ 75°.

Al2Cl6

Cl bridges are 3c–4e: two ordinary 2c–2e bonds, one of them dative from a Cl lone pair.

Not electron deficient. Al–Cl–Al is wider and Al···Al longer.

Ga2H6 (gallane)

The heavier analogue of diborane, with the same D2h H-bridged structure in the gas phase.

Isolated by Downs and co-workers only in 1989–91, nearly 80 years after B2H6.

Rule of thumb

If the bridging atom brings a lone pair, the bridge is electron-precise (3c–4e). If it brings only one orbital and one electron (H, CH3), the bridge is electron-deficient (3c–2e).

Wade (1971), ch. 5; A. D. Walsh, J. Chem. Soc. 1947, 89; Mingos (2021), Fig. 5; C. R. Pulham, A. J. Downs, M. J. Goode, D. W. H. Rankin, H. E. Robertson, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1991, 113, 5149.
Contrast electron-deficient (3c–2e) bridges in Al2Me6 and Ga2H6 with electron-precise (3c–4e) halide bridges in Al2Cl6. The rule of thumb is useful in exams.
What came next

From one molecule to a general theory

WNL

William N. Lipscomb (1919–2011)

  • From 1950, low-temperature single-crystal X-ray work by Lipscomb's group solved B4H10, B5H9, B5H11, B6H10 and B9H15.
  • With Eberhardt and Crawford (1954) he generalised the 3c–2e bond to B–H–B and B–B–B units.
  • This gave the topological (styx) theory of borane structure (Deck 4).

Nobel Prize in Chemistry, 1976, "for his studies on the structure of boranes illuminating problems of chemical bonding".

W. N. Lipscomb, Boron Hydrides, Benjamin, New York, 1963; Nobel Lecture, Science 1977, 196, 1047; Mingos (2021), pp. 11–14. Portrait: place portraits/lipscomb.jpg beside this file.
Lipscomb turned the diborane answer into a general theory: low-temperature X-ray structures of the higher boranes plus the 3c–2e bond gave the styx topology (Deck 4).
Summary

Key points

  • Boron has 3 electrons for 4 valence orbitals. Its very high ionisation energies (I1+I2+I3 = 6888 kJ mol⁻¹) make its chemistry covalent, and its hydrides are electron deficient.
  • Stock's high-vacuum line (1909–1932) made the boranes accessible: BnHn+4 and BnHn+6.
  • B2H6 has 12 valence electrons, too few for 7 or 8 two-electron links. Ionic, carbon-like and one-electron-bond models all failed.
  • Diamagnetism, zero dipole, methylation (n ≤ 4), IR (8 bands, C2 alternation), ED and NMR all point to D2h, H-bridged.
  • Metrics: B–Ht 1.19 Å, B–Hb 1.33 Å, B···B 1.77 Å, B–Hb–B 83°.
  • Bonding: 4 × (2c–2e) + 2 × (3c–2e) = 12 e.
Wade (1971), ch. 2; Mingos (2021); Greenwood & Earnshaw (1997), ch. 6.
Six points to remember. Ask students to justify each with one piece of evidence.
Check your understanding

Questions (press → to reveal each answer)

1. Why does a zero dipole moment not decide between the D3d and D2h models?
Both point groups contain an inversion centre, so both have μ = 0. It only rules out unsymmetrical (e.g. ionic) forms.
2. Methylation of B2H6 stops at Me4B2H2. What does this show?
Two hydrogens differ from the other four. Only the four terminal H are replaced, and the two bridging H remain.
3. Predict the ¹H NMR of the bridging H in B2H6 (¹¹B, I = 3/2).
Coupling to two equivalent ¹¹B nuclei: 2nI + 1 = 7 lines, intensities 1:2:3:4:3:2:1.
4. Why is the B–H distance from X-ray diffraction ≈ 10 pm shorter than from electron diffraction?
X-rays locate electron density. The bonding electron of H is displaced towards B, so the centre of charge is not at the proton.
Based on Wade (1971), ch. 2.
Give students a minute per question before revealing. Q3 tests the 2nI+1 rule; Q4 tests the X-ray versus ED distinction.
